annotations.query: What is Section 1 of BNS about?

required_points: Section 1 gives the short title, commencement, and application of the Act.
It says the Act is called the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 and explains when it comes into force and how it applies.
optional_points: It also covers extra-territorial application in some cases.
forbidden_points: Section 1 defines a specific offence.

annotations.notes: Grounded in Section 1 and its subsections.

annotations.query: Explain Section 2 of BNS in simple words.

required_points: Section 2 is the definitions section.
It explains the meanings of legal terms used throughout the Sanhita, such as act, child, counterfeit, dishonestly, document, good faith, injury, illegal, and public servant.
optional_points: It functions as the interpretation clause for the Act.
forbidden_points: Section 2 only defines one single term.

annotations.notes: Section 2 body and definitions.

annotations.query: What punishments are listed under Section 4 of BNS?

required_points: Section 4 lists the punishments under BNS.
They include death, imprisonment for life, imprisonment (rigorous or simple), forfeiture of property, fine, and community service.
optional_points: It is the general punishment provision.
forbidden_points: Section 4 defines a specific offence.

annotations.notes: Grounded only in BNS_2023.pdf and chunks.json.

annotations.query: What does Section 6 say about life imprisonment and term calculation?

required_points: Section 6 says that for calculating fractions of punishment, imprisonment for life is reckoned as twenty years unless otherwise provided.
It also notes that some sentences may be rigorous, simple, or partly both.
optional_points: Context can change the meaning in specific sections.
forbidden_points: Life imprisonment always means only twenty years in every context.

annotations.notes: Grounded only in BNS_2023.pdf and chunks.json.

annotations.query: Explain Section 14 of BNS.

required_points: Section 14 says nothing is an offence if done by a person who is bound by law to do it.
It also protects a person who, in good faith and due to a mistake of fact, believes he is legally bound to act.
optional_points: The mistake must be one of fact, not law.
forbidden_points: A mistake of law is enough under this section.

annotations.notes: Grounded only in BNS_2023.pdf and chunks.json.

annotations.query: What is the accident exception under Section 18?

required_points: Section 18 excuses an act done by accident or misfortune when there is no criminal intention or knowledge.
The act must be a lawful act done lawfully, with proper care and caution.
optional_points: If there is negligence or lack of caution, the exception may fail.
forbidden_points: Any accidental harm is automatically excused.

annotations.notes: Grounded only in BNS_2023.pdf and chunks.json.

annotations.query: What does Section 20 say about children under seven years?

required_points: Section 20 says nothing is an offence when done by a child under seven years of age.
It also points to a separate rule for children above seven and under twelve with immature understanding.
optional_points: The query focuses on the under-seven rule.
forbidden_points: A child under seven is always fully liable.

annotations.notes: Grounded only in BNS_2023.pdf and chunks.json.

annotations.query: Explain Section 22 on unsoundness of mind.

required_points: Section 22 says nothing is an offence if, at the time of doing it, a person is incapable of knowing the nature of the act or that it is wrong or contrary to law because of unsoundness of mind.
optional_points: The provision also deals with intoxication-related incapacity in the same section.
forbidden_points: Every act by a person with any mental issue is automatically excused.

annotations.notes: Grounded only in BNS_2023.pdf and chunks.json.

annotations.query: What does Section 32 say about being forced by threats?

required_points: Section 32 protects acts done under threats that create a reasonable fear of instant death.
The exception does not cover murder or offences against the State punishable with death.
optional_points: The threat must be immediate and serious.
forbidden_points: All threats create a defence in every offence.

annotations.notes: Grounded only in BNS_2023.pdf and chunks.json.

annotations.query: What is the right of private defence under Section 34?

required_points: Section 34 says nothing is an offence when done in the exercise of the right of private defence.
Section 35 says everyone has a right to defend body and property, subject to restrictions.
optional_points: The right is limited by later sections.
forbidden_points: Private defence allows unlimited force.

annotations.notes: Grounded only in BNS_2023.pdf and chunks.json.

annotations.query: When does private defence of body extend to causing death?

required_points: Section 38 says private defence of the body can extend to causing death only in serious situations such as reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt, or certain grave assaults.
Section 39 says if the case is not one of those serious categories, private defence of body does not extend to causing death, only to other harm within limits.
optional_points: The right is still subject to section 37 restrictions.
forbidden_points: Private defence of the body always allows killing the attacker.

annotations.notes: Grounded only in BNS_2023.pdf and chunks.json.

annotations.query: Explain abetment under Section 45.

required_points: Section 45 says a person abets a thing if he instigates it, joins a conspiracy for it with an act or illegal omission in pursuance, or intentionally aids it.
optional_points: Abetment can be by instigation, conspiracy, or intentional aid.
forbidden_points: Abetment requires only silent presence.

annotations.notes: Grounded only in BNS_2023.pdf and chunks.json.

annotations.query: What is criminal conspiracy under Section 61?

required_points: Section 61 defines criminal conspiracy as an agreement by two or more persons to do an illegal act, or to do a lawful act by illegal means.
For an agreement to commit an offence, the agreement itself is enough; for other conspiracies, an additional act in pursuance may be required.
optional_points: The common object matters.
forbidden_points: Criminal conspiracy needs no agreement.

annotations.notes: Grounded only in BNS_2023.pdf and chunks.json.

annotations.query: What is rape under Section 63?

required_points: Section 63 defines rape by listing specified sexual acts committed against a woman in circumstances such as against her will, without consent, or with consent obtained by fear or deception.
optional_points: The section also covers several specific consent-invalidating situations.
forbidden_points: Rape requires no issue of consent.

annotations.notes: Grounded only in BNS_2023.pdf and chunks.json.

annotations.query: What is cruelty under Section 86?

required_points: Section 86 defines cruelty for section 85.

Cruelty includes wilful conduct likely to drive the woman to suicide or cause grave injury or danger to life, limb, or health, and harassment connected with unlawful demands for property or valuable security.
optional_points: It is used to interpret the offence in section 85.
forbidden_points: Any disagreement automatically counts as cruelty.

annotations.notes: Grounded only in BNS_2023.pdf and chunks.json.

annotations.query: What does “dishonestly” mean under BNS?

required_points: ‘Dishonestly’ means doing something with the intention of causing wrongful gain to one person or wrongful loss to another.
optional_points: It focuses on intended gain or loss.
forbidden_points: Dishonestly requires deceit alone, with no gain or loss element.

annotations.notes: Grounded only in BNS_2023.pdf and chunks.json.

annotations.query: What is the meaning of wrongful gain and wrongful loss?

gold_references.label: Section 2(36)
gold_references.role: definitions of wrongful gain and wrongful loss

gold_references.label: Section 2(37)
gold_references.role: definitions of wrongful gain and wrongful loss

required_points: Wrongful gain means gain by unlawful means of property to which the person gaining is not legally entitled.
Wrongful loss means loss by unlawful means of property to which the person losing it is legally entitled.
optional_points: They are a matched pair of property concepts.
forbidden_points: Wrongful gain and loss are limited to physical injury.

annotations.notes: Grounded only in BNS_2023.pdf and chunks.json.

annotations.query: What is a document under BNS?

required_points: A document is any matter expressed or described on any substance by letters, figures, or marks, including electronic and digital records, when it is intended to be or may be used as evidence of that matter.
optional_points: Cheques, maps, plans, and powers of attorney are examples in the section.
forbidden_points: A document must always be paper only.

annotations.notes: Grounded only in BNS_2023.pdf and chunks.json.

annotations.query: What does counterfeit mean under BNS?

required_points: Counterfeit means causing one thing to resemble another with intent to practise deception, or knowing deception is likely to be practised.
optional_points: The imitation need not be exact.
forbidden_points: Counterfeit requires an exact copy.

annotations.notes: Grounded only in BNS_2023.pdf and chunks.json.

annotations.query: What does “good faith” mean under BNS?

required_points: Nothing is said to be done or believed in good faith if it is done or believed without due care and attention.
optional_points: Due care is central to the definition.
forbidden_points: Good faith means only honest intention, with no care requirement.

annotations.notes: Grounded only in BNS_2023.pdf and chunks.json.

annotations.query: Who is a public servant under BNS?

required_points: Section 2(28) gives an extended definition of public servant covering judges, government officers, court officers, armed forces officers, arbitrators, and other specified office-holders performing public duties.
optional_points: The list is illustrative of the statutory categories.
forbidden_points: Only government employees count as public servants.

annotations.notes: Grounded only in BNS_2023.pdf and chunks.json.

annotations.query: What does “injury” mean under BNS?

required_points: ‘Injury’ means any harm whatever illegally caused to any person in body, mind, reputation, or property.
optional_points: It is broad and covers several kinds of harm.
forbidden_points: Injury means only bodily harm.

annotations.notes: Grounded only in BNS_2023.pdf and chunks.json.

annotations.query: What does “illegal” mean under BNS?

required_points: ‘Illegal’ applies to anything that is an offence, prohibited by law, or that gives ground for a civil action.
optional_points: The clause also explains when a person is legally bound to do something.
forbidden_points: Illegal only means criminal.

annotations.notes: Grounded only in BNS_2023.pdf and chunks.json.

annotations.query: What is movable property under BNS?

required_points: Movable property includes property of every description except land and things attached to the earth or permanently fastened to what is attached to the earth.
optional_points: The definition is broad but excludes immovable things.
forbidden_points: Movable property includes land.

annotations.notes: Grounded only in BNS_2023.pdf and chunks.json.

annotations.query: What does “reason to believe” mean?

required_points: A person has reason to believe a thing if he has sufficient cause to believe it, but not otherwise.
optional_points: It is a cause-based standard, not mere suspicion.
forbidden_points: Reason to believe means any guess counts.

annotations.notes: Grounded only in BNS_2023.pdf and chunks.json.

annotations.query: What is consent under fear or misconception?

required_points: Consent is not valid under the Sanhita if it is given under fear of injury, or under a misconception of fact, and the person acting knows or has reason to believe this.
It is also invalid if given by a person unable to understand because of unsoundness of mind or intoxication, or by a child under twelve unless the context says otherwise.
optional_points: This is the general statutory rule on invalid consent.
forbidden_points: Any consent is valid even if given under threat.

annotations.notes: Grounded only in BNS_2023.pdf and chunks.json.

annotations.query: What is grievous hurt?

required_points: Grievous hurt means the specific severe forms of hurt listed in the section, such as emasculation, permanent loss of sight or hearing, loss or impairment of a member or joint, permanent disfiguration, fracture or dislocation, or hurt endangering life or causing severe pain or inability to follow ordinary pursuits for fifteen days.
optional_points: The section lists eight categories.
forbidden_points: Every hurt is grievous hurt.

annotations.notes: Grounded only in BNS_2023.pdf and chunks.json.

annotations.query: What is wrongful restraint?

required_points: Wrongful restraint is the voluntary obstruction of a person so as to prevent that person from proceeding in a direction in which that person has a right to proceed.
optional_points: The full definition is in section 126, not section 2.
forbidden_points: Any obstruction automatically means wrongful confinement.

annotations.notes: Grounded in Section 126.

annotations.query: What is wrongful confinement?

required_points: Wrongful confinement is wrongful restraint in such a manner as to prevent a person from proceeding beyond certain circumscribing limits.
optional_points: It is a more serious form of restraint.
forbidden_points: Wrongful confinement and wrongful restraint are the same thing.

annotations.notes: Grounded only in BNS_2023.pdf and chunks.json.

annotations.query: What is criminal force?

required_points: Criminal force is intentional use of force to a person without consent in order to commit an offence, or with intent or knowledge that the force will cause injury, fear, or annoyance.
optional_points: Force alone is not enough; the intent/knowledge element matters.
forbidden_points: Any use of force is automatically criminal force.

annotations.notes: Grounded only in BNS_2023.pdf and chunks.json.

annotations.query: What is the punishment for murder under BNS?

required_points: Whoever commits murder shall be punished with death or imprisonment for life, and also fine.
optional_points: A group murder on protected grounds is also covered in the same section.
forbidden_points: Murder is punishable only with a fine.

annotations.notes: Grounded only in BNS_2023.pdf and chunks.json.

annotations.query: What is the punishment for culpable homicide not amounting to murder?

gold_references.label: Section 105
gold_references.role: punishment for culpable homicide not amounting to murder

required_points: Culpable homicide not amounting to murder is punishable with imprisonment for life or imprisonment up to ten years and fine when intention to cause death or likely-death injury is present.
If the act is done with knowledge only, the punishment can be up to ten years and fine.
optional_points: The sentence depends on intention or knowledge.
forbidden_points: It always carries the same punishment as murder.

annotations.notes: Grounded only in BNS_2023.pdf and chunks.json.

annotations.query: What is the punishment for causing death by negligence?

gold_references.label: Section 106
gold_references.role: punishment for causing death by negligence

required_points: Causing death by a rash or negligent act not amounting to culpable homicide is punishable with imprisonment up to five years and fine.
If a registered medical practitioner causes death while performing a medical procedure, the maximum term is two years.
optional_points: If a person dies in rash and negligent driving and the offender escapes without reporting, a higher punishment can apply under the same section.
forbidden_points: Negligent death has no punishment under BNS.

annotations.notes: Grounded only in BNS_2023.pdf and chunks.json.

annotations.query: What is the punishment for rape?

required_points: The general punishment for rape is rigorous imprisonment of not less than ten years, which may extend to imprisonment for life, plus fine.
optional_points: Special aggravated situations are covered in the same section.
forbidden_points: Rape is punishable only with a short jail term or fine.

annotations.notes: Grounded only in BNS_2023.pdf and chunks.json.

annotations.query: What is the punishment for gang rape?

required_points: Gang rape is punished with rigorous imprisonment of not less than twenty years, which may extend to imprisonment for life, and fine.
Where the victim is under eighteen in a gang-rape case, the section allows imprisonment for life or death.
optional_points: Fine is intended to support the victim's medical and rehabilitation needs.
forbidden_points: Gang rape has the same punishment as ordinary rape in every case.

annotations.notes: Grounded only in BNS_2023.pdf and chunks.json.

annotations.query: What is the punishment for dowry death?

required_points: Dowry death is punished with imprisonment for a term not less than seven years, which may extend to imprisonment for life.
optional_points: The section defines dowry death by reference to death within seven years of marriage plus cruelty/harassment for dowry.
forbidden_points: Dowry death is punishable only with a small fine.

annotations.notes: Grounded only in BNS_2023.pdf and chunks.json.

annotations.query: What is the punishment for cruelty by husband or relatives?

gold_references.label: Section 85
gold_references.role: punishment for cruelty by husband or relatives

required_points: A husband or relative of a husband who subjects a woman to cruelty shall be punished with imprisonment up to three years and fine.
optional_points: Cruelty is separately defined in section 86.
forbidden_points: There is no punishment for cruelty by husband or relatives.

annotations.notes: Grounded only in BNS_2023.pdf and chunks.json.

annotations.query: What is the punishment for theft?

required_points: Whoever commits theft shall be punished with imprisonment up to three years, or with fine, or with both.
optional_points: Repeat conviction can attract a higher term under the same subsection.
forbidden_points: Theft has no punishment in BNS.

annotations.notes: Grounded only in BNS_2023.pdf and chunks.json.

annotations.query: What is the punishment for snatching?

required_points: Whoever commits snatching shall be punished with imprisonment up to three years and fine.
optional_points: Snatching is a special form of theft defined in section 304(1).
forbidden_points: Snatching is punished exactly like ordinary theft in every case.

annotations.notes: Grounded only in BNS_2023.pdf and chunks.json.

annotations.query: What is the punishment for robbery?

required_points: Whoever commits robbery shall be punished with rigorous imprisonment up to ten years and fine.
If robbery is committed on the highway between sunset and sunrise, the term may extend to fourteen years.
optional_points: Attempted robbery and robbery with hurt have separate enhanced punishments in the same section.
forbidden_points: Robbery is punishable only with a fine.

annotations.notes: Grounded only in BNS_2023.pdf and chunks.json.

annotations.query: What is the punishment for dacoity?

required_points: Whoever commits dacoity shall be punished with imprisonment for life or rigorous imprisonment up to ten years, and fine.
optional_points: If murder is committed in the course of dacoity, section 310(3) provides a harsher punishment.
forbidden_points: Dacoity is punishable only as an ordinary robbery.

annotations.notes: Grounded only in BNS_2023.pdf and chunks.json.

annotations.query: What is the punishment for criminal breach of trust?

gold_references.label: Section 316(2)
gold_references.role: punishment for criminal breach of trust

required_points: Whoever commits criminal breach of trust shall be punished with imprisonment up to five years, or fine, or both.
optional_points: Higher terms apply for carriers, clerks/servants, and public-servant/banker capacities.
forbidden_points: Criminal breach of trust has no punishment.

annotations.notes: Grounded only in BNS_2023.pdf and chunks.json.

annotations.query: What is the punishment for cheating?

required_points: Whoever cheats shall be punished with imprisonment up to three years, or fine, or both.
optional_points: More serious forms of cheating carry higher punishment in subsections (3) and (4).
forbidden_points: Cheating is always punished with imprisonment for life.

annotations.notes: Grounded only in BNS_2023.pdf and chunks.json.

annotations.query: What is the punishment for false evidence?

gold_references.label: Section 229
gold_references.role: punishment for false evidence in judicial proceedings

required_points: Intentional false evidence in a judicial proceeding is punishable with imprisonment up to seven years and fine.
If false evidence is given in a case other than a judicial proceeding, section 229(2) provides up to three years and fine.
optional_points: The offence is first defined in section 227 and fabrication is covered in section 228.
forbidden_points: Any false statement anywhere is automatically the same offence regardless of context.

annotations.notes: Grounded only in BNS_2023.pdf and chunks.json.

annotations.query: What is the punishment for criminal intimidation?

required_points: Criminal intimidation is punishable with imprisonment up to two years, or fine, or both.
Threats involving death, grievous hurt, fire, or life-imprisonment level offences carry a higher punishment under subsection (3).
optional_points: Anonymous threats have a separate enhancement under subsection (4).
forbidden_points: Criminal intimidation is not punishable.

annotations.notes: Grounded only in BNS_2023.pdf and chunks.json.

annotations.query: Someone pointed a knife at me and took my phone. What offence is this?

acceptable_references.label: Section 304
acceptable_references.role: snatching may be discussed if facts fit

required_points: Pointing a knife and taking a phone can amount to robbery because the taking is accompanied by fear of instant harm or violence.
The facts also involve theft as the underlying taking, but robbery is the stronger classification if fear or threat is proved.
optional_points: The exact classification depends on the proved facts.
forbidden_points: This is only simple theft with no robbery issue.

annotations.notes: Grounded only in BNS_2023.pdf and chunks.json.

annotations.query: Someone borrowed my phone and never returned it. What offence may apply?

gold_references.label: Section 314
gold_references.role: dishonest misappropriation of property after lawful possession

acceptable_references.label: Section 303
acceptable_references.role: theft background if taking is dishonest

required_points: If the phone was initially entrusted or lawfully obtained and then dishonestly kept or converted, criminal breach of trust can apply.
If the facts show dishonest misappropriation after lawful possession, section 314 may also be relevant.
optional_points: The exact charge depends on whether there was entrustment or only dishonest taking.
forbidden_points: A borrowed item that is never returned is always theft in every case.

annotations.notes: Grounded only in BNS_2023.pdf and chunks.json.

annotations.query: I accidentally hit a person with my car while reversing. What can happen under BNS?

gold_references.label: Section 125
gold_references.role: rash or negligent act endangering life or personal safety

acceptable_references.label: Section 106
acceptable_references.role: causing death by negligence if death occurs

required_points: If it was a true accident done in a lawful act with proper care and no criminal intent or knowledge, section 18 may excuse it.
If the driving was rash or negligent, section 125 can apply.
If the person dies, section 106 on causing death by negligence becomes relevant.
optional_points: The exact result depends on whether there was negligence and on the injury caused.
forbidden_points: Any accidental hit with a car is always excused.

annotations.notes: Grounded only in BNS_2023.pdf and chunks.json.

annotations.query: A person hit me first and I hit back to protect myself. Is it a crime?

gold_references.label: Section 35
gold_references.role: right of private defence of body and property

required_points: A person may rely on private defence if the hit back was a genuine defensive act.
The defence must stay within the limits of necessity and section 37; excessive force is not protected.
optional_points: If there was a real attack, the right can begin as soon as reasonable apprehension arises.
forbidden_points: Any retaliation after being hit is automatically lawful.

annotations.notes: Grounded only in BNS_2023.pdf and chunks.json.

annotations.query: A child below seven years damaged someone’s property. Is the child liable?

required_points: A child under seven is not liable for an act done by that child.
So damage to property by a child below seven is not an offence under this section.
optional_points: This does not say what happens for children above seven and under twelve.
forbidden_points: A child below seven can be punished like an adult.

annotations.notes: Grounded only in BNS_2023.pdf and chunks.json.

annotations.query: A person with unsound mind committed an act that caused harm. How does BNS treat this?

required_points: If, at the time of the act, the person was incapable of knowing the nature of the act or that it was wrong or contrary to law because of unsoundness of mind, the act is not an offence under section 22.
optional_points: The relevant mental condition must exist at the time of the act.
forbidden_points: Any mental disorder automatically removes liability in every case.

annotations.notes: Grounded only in BNS_2023.pdf and chunks.json.

annotations.query: Someone forced me at gunpoint to help commit a crime. Will I still be punished?

required_points: If the act was done under qualifying threats causing a reasonable fear of instant death, section 32 may excuse it.
The exception does not apply to murder or offences against the State punishable with death.
optional_points: The threat must be immediate and serious.
forbidden_points: All crimes done under pressure are excused.

annotations.notes: Grounded only in BNS_2023.pdf and chunks.json.

annotations.query: I injured someone while trying to stop a theft. Can private defence apply?

gold_references.label: Section 35
gold_references.role: right of private defence of body and property

gold_references.label: Section 41
gold_references.role: private defence of property may extend to causing death in some cases

gold_references.label: Section 42
gold_references.role: private defence of property short of death

required_points: Private defence can apply if the force used was necessary to stop theft or protect property.
The right is limited by the seriousness of the threat and by section 37.
optional_points: The exact scope depends on whether the threat is theft, robbery, mischief, or criminal trespass.
forbidden_points: You may use any level of force whenever you suspect theft.

annotations.notes: Grounded only in BNS_2023.pdf and chunks.json.

annotations.query: Someone entered my house at night to steal. Can I use private defence?

gold_references.label: Section 41
gold_references.role: private defence of property against theft or house-breaking

required_points: Private defence of property can apply against theft and, in serious cases, house-breaking after sunset and before sunrise.
The right continues while the relevant danger or offence continues.
optional_points: Section 35 also recognizes defence of property generally.
forbidden_points: A homeowner can use unlimited force simply because someone entered the house.

annotations.notes: Grounded only in BNS_2023.pdf and chunks.json.

annotations.query: A group planned to commit an offence but was caught before doing it. What offence may apply?

required_points: If two or more people agreed to commit an offence, criminal conspiracy may apply even before the offence is carried out.
For conspiracy to commit an offence, the agreement itself is the key element.
optional_points: If the planned act was not an offence, an act in pursuance may also be required.
forbidden_points: No offence can exist before the planned act is completed.

annotations.notes: Grounded only in BNS_2023.pdf and chunks.json.

annotations.query: Someone encouraged another person to commit theft. What offence may apply?

acceptable_references.label: Section 49
acceptable_references.role: punishment if the abetted offence is committed

required_points: Encouraging another person to commit theft can amount to abetment if it is instigation, conspiracy, or intentional aid.
If the theft is actually committed in consequence, section 49 may affect punishment.
optional_points: Mere presence is not enough.
forbidden_points: Encouragement can never be abetment.

annotations.notes: Grounded only in BNS_2023.pdf and chunks.json.

annotations.query: A person knowingly bought stolen property. What offence may apply?

required_points: Knowingly buying property that is stolen can amount to receiving or retaining stolen property.
The property is ‘stolen property’ if its possession was transferred by theft, extortion, robbery, cheating, or criminal misappropriation/breach of trust.
optional_points: Knowledge or reason to believe that it is stolen is important.
forbidden_points: Buying stolen property is never an offence.

annotations.notes: Grounded only in BNS_2023.pdf and chunks.json.

annotations.query: A servant stole property from their employer. What section may apply?

gold_references.label: Section 316(4)
gold_references.role: criminal breach of trust by clerk or servant

required_points: A servant who is entrusted with property and dishonestly misappropriates it can be liable for criminal breach of trust as a clerk or servant under section 316(4).
optional_points: Section 316(2) is the general rule; subsection (4) is the servant-specific aggravation.
forbidden_points: A servant taking employer property is only a civil matter.

annotations.notes: Grounded only in BNS_2023.pdf and chunks.json.

annotations.query: Someone threatened to kill me unless I paid money. What offence may apply?

required_points: Threatening to kill someone unless money is paid can amount to criminal intimidation.
If fear is used to dishonestly induce delivery of money, extortion may also apply.
optional_points: The exact section depends on whether property was actually demanded or delivered.
forbidden_points: A threat to kill for money is a harmless loophole.

annotations.notes: Grounded only in BNS_2023.pdf and chunks.json.

annotations.query: Someone spread a false statement to damage my reputation. What offence may apply?

required_points: Spreading a false statement to damage reputation can amount to defamation.
The statement must concern a person and be made with intent to harm, or knowledge/reason to believe it will harm reputation.
optional_points: The exact defences and exceptions are in later parts of the section.
forbidden_points: Any false statement is always defamation regardless of reputation harm.

annotations.notes: Grounded only in BNS_2023.pdf and chunks.json.

annotations.query: A person gave false evidence in court. What offence is this?

gold_references.label: Section 229
gold_references.role: punishment for false evidence in judicial proceedings

required_points: Giving false evidence in court is the offence of giving false evidence.
If it is given in a judicial proceeding, section 229 provides punishment up to seven years and fine.
optional_points: Section 227 defines the offence and section 229 states punishment.
forbidden_points: False evidence in court is not an offence.

annotations.notes: Grounded only in BNS_2023.pdf and chunks.json.

annotations.query: Someone forged a document to claim property. What offence may apply?

required_points: Forging a document to claim property can amount to forgery.
Section 336 covers making a false document with intent to support a claim or title or cause a person to part with property.
optional_points: Section 335 defines making a false document.
forbidden_points: Forging a property claim document is harmless if no one notices.

annotations.notes: Grounded only in BNS_2023.pdf and chunks.json.

annotations.query: A person used a fake seal to create a legal-looking document. What offence may apply?

gold_references.label: Section 341
gold_references.role: making or possessing counterfeit seal with intent to commit forgery

acceptable_references.label: Section 342
acceptable_references.role: counterfeiting device or mark used for authenticating documents

required_points: Using a fake seal to create a legal-looking document may fall under making or possessing a counterfeit seal or instrument for forgery.
Section 341 is the relevant provision when the fake seal is intended for forgery.
optional_points: Section 342 can also apply when a device or mark is used to authenticate forged documents.
forbidden_points: A counterfeit seal is never criminally relevant.

annotations.notes: Grounded only in BNS_2023.pdf and chunks.json.

annotations.query: If someone commits an act by mistake of fact, can they be protected?

gold_references.label: Section 14
gold_references.role: mistake of fact / bound by law exception

required_points: Yes, a mistake of fact can protect the person if he was acting under a legal duty or in good faith believed he was bound by law.
The protection does not apply to a mistake of law.
optional_points: The key is that the mistake is of fact, not law, and the belief is in good faith.
forbidden_points: A mistake of law is enough to excuse the act.

annotations.query: If harm is caused accidentally during a lawful act, is it still an offence?

gold_references.label: Section 18
gold_references.role: accident in doing a lawful act

gold_references.label: Section 19
gold_references.role: act likely to cause harm, but done without criminal intent, and to prevent other harm

required_points: An accidental harm is not automatically an offence.
Section 18 excuses accident or misfortune in doing a lawful act lawfully and with proper care, and section 19 excuses some harmful acts done in good faith to prevent greater harm.
optional_points: Whether the act was lawful and done with proper care matters.
forbidden_points: Any accidental harm is always punishable.

annotations.query: If an act causes slight harm, is it always punishable?

required_points: No. Section 33 says an act is not an offence merely because it causes slight harm if the harm is so slight that no person of ordinary sense and temper would complain.
So slight harm is not always punishable.
optional_points: The standard is objective and based on ordinary sense and temper.
forbidden_points: All harm, no matter how slight, is punishable.

annotations.query: When does private defence start and when does it end?

gold_references.label: Section 40
gold_references.role: commencement and continuance of right of private defence of body

gold_references.label: Section 43
gold_references.role: commencement and continuance of right of private defence of property

required_points: The right of private defence starts when a reasonable apprehension of danger arises.
For the body, it continues while that apprehension continues; for property, section 43 says it continues only while the relevant threat or offence continues.
optional_points: Different rules apply depending on whether the defence is of body or property.
forbidden_points: Private defence lasts forever once it starts.

annotations.query: Can private defence be used against a public servant?

gold_references.label: Section 37
gold_references.role: acts against which there is no right of private defence

required_points: Generally, there is no right of private defence against an act done by a public servant acting in good faith under colour of office, unless the act reasonably causes apprehension of death or grievous hurt.
The section also says private defence is unavailable when there is time to get public protection, and it cannot inflict more harm than necessary.
optional_points: Knowledge that the actor is a public servant matters.
forbidden_points: You may always use private defence against any public servant.

annotations.query: Can a person be punished for both abetment and the offence committed?

gold_references.label: Section 52
gold_references.role: abettor liable to cumulative punishment for act abetted and act done

gold_references.label: Section 49
gold_references.role: punishment of abetment if act abetted is committed

required_points: Yes. If the act done in addition to the abetted act is a distinct offence, the abettor can be punished for both.
Section 52 specifically allows cumulative punishment when the abettor is liable for both the abetted act and another distinct offence committed in consequence.
optional_points: Section 49 explains that when the abetted act is committed in consequence, punishment follows the offence unless a special provision applies.
forbidden_points: Abetment can never lead to more than one punishment.

annotations.query: Can a person be liable if the abetted act causes a different result than intended?

optional_points: The section contains an illustration where a person abets grievous hurt but death follows.
forbidden_points: An abettor is liable only for the exact result he wanted.

annotations.query: What is the difference between theft and robbery?

required_points: Theft is the dishonest taking of movable property without consent.
Robbery is theft or extortion combined with immediate force, fear, hurt, or restraint; so robbery is theft plus violence or threat of instant harm.
optional_points: Robbery is the more serious form because of the immediate force or fear element.
forbidden_points: Robbery and theft are the same.

annotations.query: What is the difference between robbery and dacoity?

required_points: Robbery is theft or extortion with immediate force or fear.
Dacoity is robbery committed or attempted conjointly by five or more persons, or with five or more persons present and aiding.
optional_points: Dacoity is group robbery with five or more participants.
forbidden_points: Dacoity can be committed by one person alone.

annotations.notes: Grounded only in BNS_2023.pdf and chunks.json.

annotations.query: What is the difference between wrongful restraint and wrongful confinement?

required_points: Wrongful restraint stops a person from going in a direction they have the right to proceed.
Wrongful confinement is wrongful restraint that blocks the person within circumscribing limits so they cannot move beyond them.
optional_points: Confinement is the more serious, enclosed form of restraint.
forbidden_points: The two offences are identical.

annotations.notes: Grounded only in BNS_2023.pdf and chunks.json.

annotations.query: What is the difference between hurt and grievous hurt?

required_points: Hurt is causing bodily pain, disease, or infirmity.

Grievous hurt is the listed set of severe injuries, such as permanent loss of sight or hearing, loss of a limb or joint function, fracture/dislocation, or hurt endangering life or causing severe pain for fifteen days.
optional_points: Grievous hurt is a legally defined subset of hurt.
forbidden_points: Any hurt is automatically grievous hurt.

annotations.query: What is the difference between murder and culpable homicide?

required_points: Culpable homicide is causing death with intention to cause death, intention to cause likely-death injury, or knowledge that death is likely.
Murder is culpable homicide with one of the additional murder conditions in section 101, such as intention to cause death or bodily injury sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death.
optional_points: All murder is culpable homicide, but not all culpable homicide is murder.
forbidden_points: Culpable homicide and murder are interchangeable in all cases.

annotations.query: What is the difference between cheating and criminal breach of trust?

required_points: Cheating involves deception that induces delivery of property, retention of property, or some act/omission causing damage or harm.
Criminal breach of trust involves property entrusted to a person who dishonestly misappropriates, uses, or disposes of it in violation of the trust or legal direction.
optional_points: Cheating starts with deception; breach of trust starts with entrustment.
forbidden_points: They require the same facts.

annotations.query: What is the difference between abetment and criminal conspiracy?

required_points: Abetment is instigation, conspiracy with an act or illegal omission in pursuance, or intentional aid.
Criminal conspiracy is an agreement by two or more persons to do an illegal act or a lawful act by illegal means.
optional_points: Conspiracy focuses on the agreement; abetment is broader and can include aid or instigation.
forbidden_points: Abetment and conspiracy are the same in every case.

annotations.notes: Grounded only in BNS_2023.pdf and chunks.json.

annotations.query: What is the difference between criminal force and assault?

required_points: Criminal force is the intentional use of force without consent for committing an offence or causing injury, fear, or annoyance.
Assault is a gesture or preparation that makes a person apprehend that criminal force is about to be used; mere words alone do not amount to assault.
optional_points: Assault is the threatened use of criminal force; criminal force is the actual use of force.
forbidden_points: Assault and criminal force are identical.

annotations.query: What is the difference between kidnapping and abduction?

Abduction under section 138 is compelling or inducing any person by force or deceit to go from any place.
optional_points: Kidnapping depends more on age/guardianship or cross-border removal; abduction depends on force or deceit.
forbidden_points: Kidnapping and abduction are the same.
